doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Slide Hampton and J.J. Johnson's last album
summary: Raph took Slide Hampton's difficult baritone horn parts home to prepare for J.J.'s last album, and he praises Hampton.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Know the repertoire, know how to play, know how to read, know how to divide notes and all of that, and how to balance and blend at the first reading. I never did. I never got music in advance. Well once or twice I did. On J.J.’s last album, on the brass orchestra, Slide Hampton called me up. I was playing baritone horn. Bruce Bonvusato and myself played baritones and they had trombones and horns and all the rest. But Slide called and he said, “Would you mind coming up to the apartment, I’d like to show you these parts.” So he showed me and I looked at it and there were a lot of finger things, I thought I think I better take this one home. And I did. And I’m glad I did because came the date I had already gotten a little bit of fingers together and I was able to get through the date. Otherwise it would have been a struggle. So that’s one of the few times that I actually did take music home.
Yeah, he writes some challenging music.

Slide is, oh he’s a marvelous, marvelous writer. I just heard him recently in Danbury with Faddis and with a wonderful piano player named Cyrus Chestnut. And Slide sounded marvelous. During the intermission he was apologizing about how rotten he sounded but that’s Slide. He doesn’t know how good he sounds. He sounded just wonderful. Playing a big horn.
